name: Christian democracy
info: Christian democracy is an ideology inspired by Christian social teaching, drawn mainly from Catholic social thought and neo-Calvinism, which arose in 19th-century Europe and shaped postwar welfare states, social market economies and the European Union.

facts.thinkers: Jacques Maritain, who comes closest to a leading thinker and tried to reconcile democracy and human rights with Thomist natural law; Emmanuel Mounier, linked to personalism; Pope Leo XIII and Pope Pius XI; Heinrich Pesch, of solidarism; Abraham Kuyper, the neo-Calvinist founder of the Anti-Revolutionary Party; Luigi Sturzo, of popularism; Frédéric Ozanam and Wilhelm von Ketteler, early social Catholics
facts.texts: Rerum Novarum (1891), Pope Leo XIII; Christianity and the Class Struggle (1891, 1950) and Calvinism: six Stone-lectures (1899), Abraham Kuyper; Quadragesimo Anno (1931), Pope Pius XI; A Personalist Manifesto (1938), Emmanuel Mounier; True Humanism (1938), The Person and the Common Good (1948) and Man and the State (1951), Jacques Maritain; Laudato Si (2015), Pope Francis
facts.ideas: personalism; solidarity; subsidiarity; sphere sovereignty; popularism; stewardship; a social market economy; the autonomy of family, church, school and other associations
facts.today: influential in Europe and Latin America and present in other parts of the world; major parties include the Christian Democratic Union of Germany, the Christian Democratic Appeal in the Netherlands, the Austrian People's Party, the Spanish People's Party, the National Action Party in Mexico and the Christian Democratic Party of Chile; many are members of the Centrist Democrat International, and European parties of the European People's Party

t: Christian democracy has drawn mainly from Catholic social teaching and neo-scholasticism, as well as the neo-Calvinist tradition, and later gained ground with Lutherans and Pentecostals.

Christian democrats are usually described as centre-left on economics and centre-right on many social and moral issues: they have often rejected liberal economics and individualism while defending private property against excessive state intervention.
Konrad Adenauer, Robert Schuman and Alcide De Gasperi, three significant men at the beginning of the European project, were all Christian democrats.
dyk: The papal encyclical Graves de communi re prohibited Christian democracy as a political label, so Luigi Sturzo used the term popularism for the same idea in the political sphere.
ev: Catholic political movements arise independently of the church to defend Catholic interests against liberal states
Pope Leo XIII issues Rerum Novarum, which gives Catholic labour movements an intellectual platform
Poland's Christian democratic movements coalesce into the Christian Democratic Party
Pope Pius XI issues Quadragesimo Anno on the 40th anniversary of Rerum Novarum
The Centre Party and the Christian Social People's Service sign the Enabling Act after the Nazis take power, and both then dissolve
The Popular Republican Movement becomes the largest party in the French parliament
The European People's Party is founded, after the European Union of Christian Democrats of 1965
Corneliu Coposu re-enrols his party in Romania as the Christian Democratic National Peasants' Party

sections.origins:
The origins of Christian democracy go back to the French Revolution, when French republicanism and the Catholic Church were deeply hostile to one another. The revolutionary governments attacked the church, confiscated its lands, persecuted its priests and attempted to establish new religions, first the Cult of Reason and then the Cult of the Supreme Being. In the decades that followed, the church saw the rise of liberalism as a threat to Catholic values, and it saw capitalism, industrialisation and urbanisation as destroying traditional communal and family life. According to the Catholic Church, liberal economics promoted selfishness and materialism, and for much of the 19th century the church was hostile to democracy and liberalism.

That hostility was challenged by liberal Catholics, who believed the alliance between the church and aristocracy was a barrier to the church's mission. They wanted Catholics involved in parties, public action and parliamentarianism, although at first this was not an endorsement of democracy; Félicité de La Mennais, a leading figure, later became more accepting of it. Frédéric Ozanam, the founder of the Society of St Vincent de Paul, criticised economic liberalism and the commodification of labour and argued that labour associations and state intervention were needed; Luigi Sturzo credited him as the first Christian democrat. In Germany, Wilhelm von Ketteler encouraged Catholics to accept the modern state and argued for productive associations with profit sharing, Christian trade unions and general workers' rights.
sections.ideas:
No single author has been recognised by all Christian democrats as the leading thinker, but Jacques Maritain comes closest. Thomas Aquinas and his thought on natural law, human dignity and the family were the philosophical roots, revived in the neo-scholasticism that followed Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Aeterni Patris; the neo-Calvinist strand relied on John Calvin's ideas of the sovereignty of God and common grace. Academics have named several key ideas. Personalism, generally linked to Emmanuel Mounier, holds that humans are free beings with dignity and political rights, to be used for the common good, and it opposes both individualist and collectivist views of humanity. Pluralism has a vertical sense in subsidiarity, under which civil issues are first addressed at the lowest level of government, and a horizontal sense in sphere sovereignty, under which sectors such as family, education, economy and state each have autonomy and responsibility over their own sphere. The other ideas are solidarity, popularism and stewardship.

Christian democrats are usually socially conservative, generally sceptical of abortion and same-sex marriage, and they stress the individual's duties to a community. They also emphasise social justice, a welfare state, labour unions and regulation of market forces, and most European Christian democrats reject class struggle in favour of co-determination. Over time they moved from solidarism to the social market economy, which rests on a free price system and private property but adds a comprehensive social welfare system.
sections.spread:
In the 1870s Catholic political movements arose independently of the church to defend Catholic interests against liberal states, especially over education. The parties that came from them included the Centre Party in Germany, the Catholic Party in Belgium, Catholic parties in the Netherlands and the Christian Social Party in Austria. At first they accepted the church's anti-liberal beliefs, but the effect of electoral politics pushed them to accept liberal democracy and to turn to voters rather than the church for legitimacy. Protestant confessional politics was wider and more varied. In the Netherlands, Abraham Kuyper founded the neo-Calvinist Anti-Revolutionary Party; in Germany the Lutheran Adolf Stoecker established the Christian Social Party. Rerum Novarum in 1891 was the catalyst for the beginning of Christian democracy in France, Italy and Austria.

After the Second World War, Christian democratic parties took shape in Western Europe, and in Germany Lutheran ordoliberals joined Catholics to form the Christian Democratic Union. In Sweden the Christian Democrats were founded in 1964 amongst Pentecostals. In Latin America early parties, formed in the early 20th century, were generally conservative and aimed to protect the interests of the Catholic church; after the Second Vatican Council of 1961 to 1963 Christian democrats became more progressive. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, Christian democratic parties made electoral gains in Central and Eastern Europe.
sections.power:
Between the 1940s and 1990s Christian democratic parties were in power across Western Europe: in Germany for 36 years out of 50, in Italy for 47 out of 52, in Belgium for 47 out of 53 and in the Netherlands for 49 out of 53. In Italy the Christian Democratic Party led the coalition government under Alcide De Gasperi, and in France the Popular Republican Movement became the largest party in parliament in 1946. They built corporatist welfare states, pressed for works councils and workers on boards, and encouraged regionalism in Germany, Italy and Belgium. Konrad Adenauer, Robert Schuman and De Gasperi were significant at the beginning of the European project, and when the Rome Treaty was signed Christian democrats led the governments of four of the six countries.

The record in the interwar years was mixed. Corporatism, which the encyclical Quadragesimo Anno subjected to subsidiarity, inspired authoritarian and fascist regimes in Austria, France, Spain, Portugal and Germany, and it fell out of political debate for that association. Sturzo's Italian People's Party was disbanded by the fascists. In Germany the Centre Party and the Christian Social People's Service signed the Enabling Act in 1933 and then dissolved; in Austria many Christian Socials helped build an authoritarian state. Stoecker, when his pro-worker policies failed to win the working class, turned to anti-Semitism. In Latin America, COPEI helped establish democratic Venezuela and the Christian Democratic Party in Chile was the main opposition to Pinochet.
sections.critiques:
The church itself resisted the early Catholic political movements, seeing them as a challenge to its control of the laity. In Graves de communi re the pope protested against the use of Christian democracy as a political label and preferred it as a description of a social movement. Some academics consider the Catholic parties of the early 20th century essentially Catholic rather than Christian democratic, while others count the Italian People's Party and the Popular Democratic Party in France as Christian democratic.

The Christian democratic stress on class mediation was challenged in Latin America by liberation theology, which stressed class conflict. Social democrats were hostile to the European Communities until at least the mid-1980s; in the 1970s Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme called the European Commission conservative, capitalist, clerical and colonialist. Beginning in the 1980s European Christian democratic parties partly adopted neoliberal policies, and in Latin America the acceptance of neoliberal policies in the 1980s led to later electoral losses. The 2008 financial crisis is said to have shown flaws in Christian democratic welfare. The Christian democratic status of some parties is also disputed: Turkey's Justice and Development Party moved towards the tradition, but the link is questioned, and Hungary's Fidesz was part of the European People's Party from 2004 to 2021, while its leader Viktor Orbán claimed Hungary to be a Christian democracy.
sections.legacy:
Christian democratic parties no longer have as much power in European politics. In Italy the Christian democratic party collapsed, and in France the Christian democrats were absorbed into Gaullist parties. The reasons for the decline are said to be several: European secularisation and the loss of a voting base, the death of communism and the rise of neoliberalism, the 2008 financial crisis, and pressure from immigration and populism, which leaves the movement torn between the right's call for restrictions, business calls for an open labour market and the religious call for more charity to immigrants. Some parties, particularly in Europe, no longer emphasise religion and have become more secular, while minor parties such as the Christian Union joined the European Christian Political Movement.

The Centrist Democrat International, formerly the Christian Democratic International, is the second-largest international political organisation in the world, after the Socialist International, and the European People's Party forms the largest group in the European Parliament. The ideas of subsidiarity and personalism are embedded in the European Union. Many Muslim parties in Muslim countries have looked to the tradition for inspiration, among them parties in Indonesia and the Philippines that have joined the Centrist Democrat International. In the United States there has been no major Christian democratic movement; Jacques Maritain saw America as the realisation of the ideal, and the American Solidarity Party is a minor party that identifies as Christian democratic.

summary: Christian democracy is an ideology inspired by Christian social teaching, drawn mainly from Catholic social thought and neo-Calvinism. Christian democrats led postwar Western and Southern Europe in building welfare states and constructing the European Union, and their parties remain influential in Europe and Latin America.
references: Michael P. Fogarty, Christian democracy in Western Europe, 1820–1953 (Routledge & Paul, 1957)
Stathis N Kalyvas, The Rise of Christian Democracy in Europe (Cornell University Press, 1996)
Hans Maier, Revolution and church; the early history of Christian democracy, 1789–1901 (University of Notre Dame Press, 1969)
Kees van Kersbergen, Social Capitalism: A Study of Christian Democracy and the Welfare State (Routledge, 2003)
Michael Gehler, Political Catholicism in Europe 1918–1945 (Routledge, 2004)
notes: Start: 1891 (Rerum Novarum, which the article calls the catalyst for Christian democracy in France, Italy and Austria); circa true because the article traces the origins to the French Revolution and dates the first Catholic political movements to the 1870s.
Event '1976': the article says the European Union of Christian Democrats appeared in 1965 and the European People's Party in 1976; the 1965 date is given in the label.

The article says the Christian Social People's Service and the Centre Party 'would summarily dissolve' after signing the Enabling Act, but gives no year for the dissolutions; I dated only the Act (1933, when the Nazis attained power).
The 'Corneliu Coposu 1990' event: the article gives 1990 for the re-enrolment as the Christian Democratic National Peasants' Party.

Wording of the Poland and Hungary sections follows the article; I left out the detailed party lists for Poland, Russia, Australia, Canada, Greece, the United Kingdom and South Korea, and the recent items (2023, 2025) as present politics.

Section 'critiques': the article has no dedicated critique section; the material is assembled from its statements on church resistance, definitional disputes, decline and the neoliberal turn. 'Orbán claimed Hungary to be a Christian democracy' is placed under disputes only as the article's fact, with no verdict.

The article's heading 'Neo-scholasticism' says Aquinas argued public power could appropriate private resources; I left that out. The article's statement that Catholic Action 'would act as an anti-fascist force' was also left out.
Possible internal oddity: the article says Kuyper's Christian Social Congress was in 1891 and gives the Anti-Revolutionary Party as founded by him but no founding year; none is stated.
